title: Frozen shoulder: managing pain and recovering movement
intro: Frozen shoulder, also called adhesive capsulitis, causes gradually increasing pain and restricted movement. Sleep, dressing and reaching can become difficult. Other conditions also cause shoulder pain, so persistent symptoms need assessment rather than a diagnosis based on an online exercise video.

sections.heading: Confirm what is limiting movement
paragraphs: A clinician asks about the onset, injuries, previous surgery and conditions such as diabetes. They check movement both when you move the arm yourself and when they gently assist it. Examination helps distinguish joint stiffness from other shoulder problems. Scans are selected to clarify uncertain findings or exclude another cause; they are not automatically necessary.

sections.heading: Recognize symptoms needing prompt assessment
paragraphs: A shoulder that becomes deformed or impossible to move after an injury needs urgent assessment. Fever with a hot, red joint, or new weakness or numbness also needs prompt medical attention. Shoulder pain accompanied by chest discomfort, breathlessness, sweating or collapse may be an emergency: contact emergency services rather than assuming it is frozen shoulder.

sections.heading: Adapt daily activities and move gently
paragraphs: Choose clothing that is easy to put on, keep frequently used objects within reach and support the arm comfortably with a pillow at night. Continue gentle movement within an agreed comfortable range. Complete immobilization can worsen stiffness, while forceful stretching can increase pain. A physiotherapist can adapt exercises to your symptoms and stage of recovery.

sections.heading: Discuss pain relief and injections
paragraphs: Ask a clinician or pharmacist which pain medicine is suitable alongside your other conditions and treatments. Anti-inflammatory medicines may be unsuitable with stomach ulcers, kidney disease or certain blood-thinning medicines. A steroid injection can provide short-term relief for some people but does not immediately restore movement. Discuss risks and, if you have diabetes, a plan for possible temporary changes in blood glucose.

sections.heading: Review progress rather than promise a deadline
paragraphs: Recovery often takes months and sometimes years; improvement is not identical for everyone. Agree goals such as sleeping better or reaching a shelf, and review persistent or worsening symptoms. Exercise should not be forced through severe pain. Specialist procedures or surgery are reserved for selected cases after discussion of likely benefit, uncertainty and risks; most people do not need surgery.

examples.title: Dressing becomes a useful goal
examples.text: In this hypothetical example, Mira struggles to put on a jacket. After assessment, she chooses easier clothing and follows gentle prescribed exercises, using dressing and sleep as progress measures instead of forcing the arm behind her back.

examples.title: Planning an injection with diabetes
examples.text: In this hypothetical example, Arben asks about an injection because pain interrupts sleep. He discusses expected short-term benefit, glucose monitoring and when to contact his diabetes team before deciding.
